title: Tabitha, arise (Acts 9:32–43)
hookLine: no eulogy, just a pile of coats held up by the women who wore them
tomorrow: a soldier and a hungry man on a roof. who sent for whom?

lines: A TABLE OF THINGS SHE MADE.
cards: At some memorials there's a table: photos, a favorite mug, a jersey, the quilt she made. Objects say who someone was faster than a speech can. Acts tells a story like that.

In Joppa lives "a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas," and Acts gives her life one line: "this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did." She falls sick and dies.
Her friends lay her in an upper room and send for Peter. When he arrives, nobody gives a speech.

teach.h: THE WIDOWS HOLD UP THE COATS.
teach.b: Today's question: what does a faithful life look like from the outside? Acts answers with clothes. "All the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them."
They don't describe her goodness; they hold it up, stitches you can see.
Then Peter sends everyone out, kneels, prays, and says, "Tabitha, arise." "And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up." Jewish tradition answers the same question with clothes too.
In the Talmud, a rabbi asks how a person can walk after God, as the Torah commands. His answer: follow God's ways.

teach.h: THE TALMUD: CLOTHE, AS GOD CLOTHED.
teach.b: As God clothed the naked, so you clothe the naked; as God visits the sick, so you visit the sick.

And the first example comes from Genesis: "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them." A coat sewn for someone in need is holy work on both pages. Here's the honest difference.
For the rabbis, clothing others is walking in God's own ways, a commandment of the Torah given to the Jewish people.

teach.h: SAME KIND OF COAT, DIFFERENT STORY.
teach.b: Acts tells Tabitha's story as part of the story of Jesus, and its high point is Peter, praying, calling her back to life.
Not the same story. The same kind of coat.

how: Some churches keep a closet of coats for neighbors in need, and some sewing circles take the name Dorcas from this story.

o: a disciple at Joppa known for the coats she made
a prophetess who waited in the Temple
a seller of purple cloth who hosted Paul

games.q: Joppa, and a neighbor's page — tap the pairs.
p: clothe the naked, as God did

s: the widows described Tabitha in a speech
they showed Peter the coats and garments she made. no speech at all.
clothing the naked as holy work is an idea only Christians have
the Talmud teaches it as walking in God's ways, starting from God clothing Adam and Eve.
a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas.

games.q: a synagogue near your church runs a winter coat drive and invites your youth group to help. a friend asks if that's 'mixing religions.' what fits today's lesson?
o: help: clothing people is shared ground, and each can keep its own reasons.
skip it: Christians should only give through their own church.
help, but only once both groups agree they believe the same things.
games.why: the widows held up Tabitha's coats, and the Talmud calls clothing the naked walking in God's ways. the work is shared; the stories behind it stay honestly different.

practice: Find one piece of clothing near you: a jacket with a loose button, a sweater you no longer wear. Hold it through the sit and feel the seams, the work someone's hands put into it.
Before the bell ends, decide one thing: mend it, or give it to someone who'd wear it.

wordCard.voice: Tabitha. A disciple of Joppa, also called Dorcas, remembered by the coats she made.

orig.note: Tabitha as written in the Greek of Acts 9:36, which then gives her name in Greek: Dorcas.

carryVoice: Keep this one: full of good works, the kind you can hold up. Go well.
